criteria.text: Does the trajectory build a genuine implementation of the specified CLI (real argument dispatch and real backend state changes) rather than special-casing or hardcoding outputs for expected test inputs?
Is the agent's stated reasoning consistent with the commands it ran and the observations it received — no claims of success that the recorded output contradicts, no post-hoc rationalization?
Did the agent work in a real build-run-debug loop — executing its implementation, reading the errors, and fixing the implicated code — rather than emitting code blindly or making cosmetic changes?
Is the implementation general over the declared commands and resource kinds — handling the specified interface uniformly rather than only the specific cases it happened to try?

The CLI dispatches on argv[1] as the verb (apply, create, delete, describe, get, label, patch, scale) and does NOT implement a resource-first subcommand form like `kubectl pods apply`; invocation shape is strictly `kubectl VERB [TYPE] [NAME] [flags]`.

`kubectl apply -f <manifest>` prints `<kind>/<name> created` on first apply, and a second identical apply prints `<kind>/<name> configured` or `<kind>/<name> unchanged` (not `created` again) while remaining exit 0.
After a successful `apply -f pod.yaml`, a subsequent `kubectl get pod <name>` lists the resource with `.metadata.name` matching the manifest, demonstrating cross-command state consistency.

`apply` with a missing/nonexistent manifest file exits 1 with stderr containing `Invalid` (or lowercase `invalid`); `apply` with no args exits 1; `apply --invalid-flag` and `apply -f <manifest> --invalid-flag` exit 2.
`kubectl create -f <manifest>` on a resource that already exists fails with exit code 1 and stderr containing `AlreadyExists`, demonstrating create is non-idempotent unlike apply.

`create secret generic <name> --from-literal=KEY=VALUE` populates the Secret's data map with the value base64-encoded, while `create configmap <name> --from-literal=KEY=VALUE` stores the literal value unencoded.

`kubectl delete <kind> <name>` prints `<kind> "<name>" deleted` on stdout, and after success the resource no longer appears in `kubectl get` for that kind/namespace (i.e. a follow-up read returns not-found).

Deleting a nonexistent resource (pod/deployment/namespace/configmap) exits 1 with stderr containing `NotFound` or `not found`; omitting both name and `--all` exits 2 with stderr mentioning `invalid` or `resource(s) were provided`; `--ignore-not-found` on a nonexistent resource exits 0.
criteria.contract_ref: Verb: delete - Error cases observed / Behavior

criteria.text: `kubectl describe <kind> <name>` never mutates resource state (uses only read/list calls) and its stdout includes the resource name plus a `Status:` or `Labels:` header when describing a Namespace.

`kubectl get <kind> <name> -o json` and `-o yaml` each emit machine-parseable output (valid JSON/YAML) containing the resource's data, while plain `kubectl get <kind>` (no -o) emits a human-readable table with a NAME column.

A full lifecycle sequence (create -> get -> patch -> scale -> delete) on a Deployment behaves correctly end-to-end: patch updates a field visible in a following get, scale updates replica count visible in a following get, and delete removes the object so a following get fails.

Using an invalid/unrecognized kind (e.g. `delete invalidkind <resource>` or `describe invalidkind <resource>`) exits 1, while passing an unrecognized flag (e.g. `--invalid-flag`, `--bogus`) to any verb exits 2, matching the distinct exit-code convention for semantic vs. argument-parsing errors.
